title: Working with magnification
subtitle: When to use a magnifier and how to set one up for embroidery.
excerpt: Magnification helps with fine detail work, thread counting, and small-scale stitching. A clip-on hoop magnifier, a freestanding lens, or reading glasses can all reduce eye strain during long sessions. This reading covers the options and how to use them without losing your bearings.
sourceNotes: Ergonomics guidance for needlework synthesised from contemporary practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Any lens-based tool that enlarges the view of fine needlework. Options include clip-on hoop magnifiers, freestanding floor or table lamps with a built-in lens, and wearable magnifying glasses. Used to reduce eye strain and improve accuracy on small-scale work.

content.text: are not only for those with poor eyesight. Anyone stitching fine detail over long sessions benefits from a lens that removes the need to lean in close. Reducing that forward lean alone relieves neck and shoulder strain.

A clip-on hoop magnifier fastens to the outer ring of the embroidery hoop and swings into position when needed. It keeps the lens at a fixed distance from the work and leaves both hands free. This is the most practical option for most stitchers.
A freestanding magnifying lamp combines an LED light and a lens in a floor or desk stand. The light eliminates shadows under the lens. These are the professional standard in goldwork and needlelace.

Wearable magnifying glasses leave the hands completely free but take some adjustment. The fixed focal length means the work must be held at exactly the right distance. A neck frame or headband magnifier works similarly.

For general embroidery, 1.5x to 2x magnification is enough. Higher magnification narrows the field of view, making it hard to see the context of the stitch. Use higher magnification only for very small detail work such as miniature cross stitch on 22-count Hardanger.

A lens without good lighting makes things worse, not better. Place a bright task light on the opposite side to your stitching hand so it illuminates the work surface from an angle, not from directly above. This shows the texture of the stitches rather than flattening them.
